articles.title: Algeria faces calls to drop death penalty plans after wildfires
articles.summary: Rights group warns Algeria could exploit proposed death penalty laws to suppress domestic political opposition.
articles.body:
Amnesty International urges Algeria to halt plans to expand death penalty and resume executions following wildfires, citing human rights concerns.

Algeria has not carried out an execution in over 30 years, but President Tebboune seeks to broaden capital punishment sentencing in response to recent devastating wildfires.

Amnesty accuses Algerian authorities of using expanded death penalty to target political opposition groups, calling for accountability for climate catastrophes instead of pursuing alleged arsonists.

Amnesty International has urged Algeria to abandon plans to expand the death penalty and resume executions, following presidential moves to make wildfire arson a capital crime.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the human rights organisation called for an immediate halt to President Abdelmadjid Tebboune's directives. Algeria has not carried out an execution in more than 30 years.

The push to broaden capital punishment sentencing gained momentum following devastating wildfires that killed at least 12 people and injured 54 others last month.

The flames wiped out entire villages across the Kabylie region and other parts of northeastern Algeria, the statement said.

In the aftermath of the fires, Tebboune instructed Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa to amend the law to include arson as well as "child abductors and abusers".

Anyone sentenced to death could exercise their right to appeal before being executed, Tebboune said.

Amnesty accused Algerian authorities of using the proposed expanded death penalty to target political opposition groups.

The rights group said authorities arrested 20 people pending investigations for arson and subversion – a potentially terrorism-related charge – between July 26 and September 10.

During the 2021 wildfires that left 90 dead, the government prosecuted scores of people on terrorism-related charges, blaming the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylie (MAK), an opposition group that the government classifies as a terrorist organisation.

Amnesty urged the government to address the root cause of the climate catastrophes instead of pursuing "arsonists".

"Accountability for the devastating loss of life caused by wildfires cannot be reduced to pursuing alleged perpetrators of arson," the human rights group stated.

articles.title: IDF kills senior Hamas Rafah Brigade commander  Nael Abu Obeid in Gaza Strip strike
articles.summary: The target of the strike was Nael Abu Obeid, the commander of Hamas’s Rafah Brigade, who replaced his predecessor, Mohammad Shabanah, who was killed by the I...
articles.body:
IDF and ISA killed Hamas’s Rafah Brigade commander, Nayal Abu Obeid, in a strike in the southern Gaza Strip on September 15, 2026.

Abu Obeid replaced his predecessor, Mohammad Shabanah, who was killed by the IDF in May 2025, and was a key figure among Hamas leaders, directing terror attacks against Israeli troops.

The IDF also announced the killing of the commander of Hamas's Jabaliya Battalion, Ahmad Batash, in a strike in the northern Gaza Strip, who was responsible for managing logistics for the Izzadin al-Qassam Brigades Northern Gaza Brigade.

The target of the strike was Nael Abu Obeid, the commander of Hamas's Rafah Brigade, who replaced his predecessor, Mohammad Shabanah, who was killed by the IDF in May 2025.

The IDF and Shin Bet (Israeli Security Agency) issued a joint statement on Tuesday, saying that they killed Hamas's Rafah Brigade commander, Nael Abu Obeid, in a strike in the southern Gaza Strip.

Obeid replaced his predecessor, Mohammad Shabanah, who was killed by the IDF in May 2025.

Abu Obeid was a key figure among Hamas leaders, according to a statement from the IDF, and previously served as the deputy commander of the Rafah Brigade and commander of the Tel al-Sultan and Yibna Battalions.

During his time as the Rafah Brigade commander, Abu Obeid directed terror attacks against Israeli troops and offensives against IDF troops.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz confirmed the strike, saying that "our message is clear: no terrorist is immune, and Hamas will not be in Gaza."

In a statement announcing Abu Obeid's death, the IDF said they "remain deployed in the area in accordance with the agreement and will continue to operate to remove any threat."

IDF kills commander of Hamas' Jabaliya Battalion

Earlier on Tuesday, the IDF announced that it had, in coordination with Shin Bet, killed the commander of Hamas's Jabaliya Battalion in a strike in the northern Gaza Strip on Monday night.

The terrorist, identified as Ahmad Batash, was responsible for managing logistics for the Izzadin al-Qassam Brigades Northern Gaza Brigade and was an integral part of supplying weapons and equipment to Hamas terrorists in the region.

Last Thursday, the IDF and Shin Bet killed Muhammad Yazouri in the Khan Yunis area. Yazouri served as commander of Hamas's Khan Yunis Brigade in the terrorist organization's military wing in the Gaza Strip.

Yazouri was appointed to the position after holding a series of roles in the brigade, including deputy commander of the Khan Yunis Brigade, commander of the brigade's combat support battalion, and head of its intelligence department. In his role, he was responsible for managing the activities of the brigade's terrorists and directing them in advancing and carrying out terror plots against IDF forces and Israeli civilians.

Jonah Davidov contributed to this report.

articles.summary: Pesquisadora brasileira no Vale do Silício aproveitou conhecimento adquirido em projeto financiado pelo governo dos Estados Unidos para desenvolver sensores e aplicá-los em pesquisas médicas.
articles.body:
Uma tecnologia criada inicialmente para ajudar a monitorar soldados expostos a explosões passou a ser usada em pesquisas para melhorar exames de crianças com câncer. A trajetória faz parte da história da brasileira Ana Cláudia Arias, pesquisadora que construiu sua carreira entre empresas de tecnologia e universidades dos Estados Unidos.

A história começou quando Ana se formou em física e foi trabalhar em uma grande empresa no Vale do Silício, na Califórnia. Logo no início da carreira, recebeu do chefe um incentivo que, segundo ela, resume parte da cultura de inovação da região: “Eu espero que você use 20% do seu tempo para desenvolver ideias sobre as quais eu não tenho ideia.”

Na época, o governo americano financiava projetos de diferentes tipos, muitos deles ligados ao Departamento de Defesa. Foi nesse contexto que Ana teve a ideia de desenvolver um dispositivo que pudesse ser colocado no capacete de soldados.

O equipamento reunia uma série de sensores com o objetivo de monitorar o ambiente e identificar se os militares haviam sido expostos a explosões.

A experiência com os sensores acabou abrindo caminho para novos projetos.

Depois de trabalhar no projeto, Ana abriu a própria empresa, voltada ao desenvolvimento de sensores para a agricultura.

A tecnologia era utilizada para medir condições como luz e água no campo.

Mais tarde, ela foi contratada como pesquisadora da Universidade de Berkeley, onde montou um laboratório de pesquisa.

Foi ali que decidiu levar para a medicina o conhecimento adquirido com os sensores usados no projeto militar.

Com seus alunos, Ana passou a desenvolver uma tecnologia para ser aplicada em exames de ressonância magnética de crianças, especialmente aquelas que precisam passar pelo procedimento durante o tratamento de doenças como o câncer.

O objetivo é reduzir a necessidade de anestesia geral durante o procedimento.

A ideia aproveita o mesmo princípio dos sensores desenvolvidos anteriormente, mas agora voltado para uma aplicação médica.

A tecnologia é produzida dentro do próprio laboratório por meio de uma impressora, o que também reduz a dependência de componentes fabricados na China.

articles.title: Iran war increasing inflation, straining US munitions: congressional report
articles.summary: Report by nonpartisan research body finds that replenishing depleted munitions stockpiles could take up to five years.
articles.body:
The US war on Iran is worsening inflation and straining the country’s munitions stockpiles, a report from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) has found.

The report, released on Tuesday, found that the cost of the six-month war has reached $38bn and is expected to rise by $3bn per month. The war is projected to increase inflation by 0.5 percentage points in the first three months of 2027.

“Donald Trump’s disastrous war in Iran has already taken the lives of brave American servicemembers and left others wounded,” Brendan Boyle, a top Democrat on the US House of Representatives Budget Committee who requested the study, said in a statement.

“Beyond that human toll, this nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs.”

The report comes as the Trump administration faces growing criticism over the unpopular war, launched by the US and Israel in February. The conflict has caused disruptions to the global energy market and contributed to rising prices as voters express concern over the cost of living ahead of the November midterm elections .

The CBO estimate is in line with those offered by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth during congressional testimony in July, during which he placed the cost of the war at $37.5bn. Hegseth urged Congress to approve a dramatic increase in the US military budget, already the largest in the world by a significant margin.

The Pentagon chief also slammed critics of the war during the heated testimony, denying that the conflict, which Trump initially estimated would last several weeks, was turning into a “quagmire”.

Reports have also found that the war has exhausted US supplies of key munitions, stretching the military’s ability to fulfil commitments in other parts of the world. The CBO report estimated that it could take up to five years to replenish US munitions stockpiles.

The report does not include borrowing costs associated with the war or Iranian attacks that have hammered US military installations in the Middle East.

The Trump administration has angrily denied reports on flagging munitions stockpiles and continued to argue that the war is worth the cost.

“With the temporary exception of Oil, prices are coming down sharply, and Oil will drop like a rock as soon as the Military Conflict with Iran is over, and that will not be long,” Trump said in a social media post on Monday.

The CBO read-out comes one day after a report on the war compiled by inspectors general at the Pentagon, a government watchdog, detailed munitions shortfalls and production bottlenecks, along with the loss of dozens of US aircraft during the war.

“We have everything required to strike at the time and place of the president’s choosing,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said after reports of munitions shortfalls.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi drone headed for Mecca
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia says it intercepted a drone before it entered Islam’s holiest city, calling pilgrims’ security a ‘red line’
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia has said that a drone launched by the Houthis towards Mecca has been intercepted and destroyed, in an escalation that could threaten the holy city.

The Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, Turki al-Maliki, said Royal Saudi Air Defence Forces intercepted the hostile drone before it entered the restricted airspace on Tuesday evening.

Al-Maliki condemned the incident as an attempt to frighten worshippers and harm civilians, warning that the security of the two holy mosques and pilgrims is a “red line”.

The Houthis have previously denied targeting Mecca, saying that they do not target holy sites.

Saudi Arabia issued a security alert on Tuesday in the holy city of Mecca for the first time since the Houthis last attempted to target the sacred area in 2017.

The alert of potential danger in Mecca was swiftly lifted after a few minutes. The same alert was activated for Taif and Jeddah, Saudi Arabia’s second-largest city.

In a statement to Yemen’s SABA news agency on Tuesday, a Houthi military source strongly rejected the claim that Houthi forces pose a threat to the city of Mecca or other Islamic holy sites.

“We categorically deny that there is any threat from Yemen directed at the city of Mecca or any other holy sites,” the source said, condemning what he described as “misinformation”.

The latest attacks mark a sharp resurgence in a conflict dating to 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen after the Houthis seized Sanaa and ousted the internationally recognised government.

A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 largely halted Houthi attacks on Saudi territory, but hostilities have escalated again since the group declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in July and gained control of critical nodes on the country’s Bab al-Mandeb coastline.

In early September, the Iran-aligned group launched missiles and drones at sites across Saudi Arabia, marking a drastic escalation in the fighting. Riyadh has accused the Houthi rebels of launching attacks on civilian and economic sites in the kingdom.

The Saudi-led coalition said it will respond “firmly” to Houthi strikes on urban areas that injured 13 people in the Saudi cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif on Tuesday.

This was the first time in nearly a decade that a security alert had been activated in Mecca.

Mecca is home to the Kaaba, Islam’s holiest site. Two billion Muslims around the world face the Kaaba during their daily prayers.

This year, Saudi Arabia welcomed around 1.7 million Muslims for the Hajj season in late May, while the country was vulnerable to direct strikes.

Hajj is considered one of the five pillars of Islam, necessary for Muslims to fulfil once in their lifetime.

Throughout the year, millions of pilgrims travel to Mecca to perform the optional Umrah pilgrimage.

Last autumn, Mecca welcomed more than 11.7 million pilgrims for Umrah between September and October 2025.

Hajj has only been restricted during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, when Saudi Arabia barred foreign Muslims from performing the pilgrimage to help prevent the spread of the virus.

It remains to be seen if the attacks on Saudi Arabia will affect pilgrimage to Mecca.

articles.title: Ms Rachel says backlash over her Gaza posts 'doesn't faze' her as she calls out celebrity silence
articles.summary: Children's YouTuber Ms. Rachel told Rolling Stone that backlash over her Gaza posts no longer fazes her after being accused of pushing anti-Israel messaging.
articles.body: Children's YouTuber star Ms. Rachel told Rolling Stone magazine on Tuesday that the backlash she received for her social media posts on Gaza "doesn't faze" her too much anymore. The magazine reported that although Ms. Rachel, whose real name is Rachel Griffin Accurso, has spoken out on other political issues such as the Trump administration's deportation policies or LGBTQ activism, her comments on the Israel-Hamas war drew the most "aggressive criticism." She remarked that the backlash surprised her initially. "I thought everyone hated me at one point," Accurso said. "People on the ground in Gaza are risking their lives all the time to help kids. I can do it from Manhattan." Fox News Digital reached out to Accurso for comment but did not immediately receive a response. CHILDREN'S YOUTUBE STAR 'MS. RACHEL' TALKS TO ANTI-ISRAEL REPORTER ABOUT GAZA POSTS The article came days after Accurso accused celebrities who haven't spoken out about Gaza of having a racial double standard in how they value children. "They probably would say something if these kids were White and from a different place. Please stop being racist and risk something," Accurso said on Instagram. She was also one of several prominent progressives who called out singer Ed Sheeran following Macklemore's removal as the opening act for his tour after he repeatedly called for a "Free Palestine" and performed his anti-Israel song "Hind’s Hall" during his act. "Ed Sheeran had an opportunity [to] show that we won't be bullied into punishing people for supporting Palestine. Instead, he caved to people who refuse to accept what the world knows. A genocide is happening in Gaza. We all need to speak out against it," Accurso wrote. "If more than 20,000 White children were killed in another part of the world, everyone would be shouting about it at their concerts," she added. "Treating some children’s lives as less worthy of outrage is racist. Silence during a genocide is not neutral." MS RACHEL CONFRONTED ON ACCUSING ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE' IN PARK INTERACTION WITH PODCASTER Accurso has been criticized by pro-Israel organizations and groups that say her posts have shared anti-Israel propaganda by repeatedly accusing the Jewish nation of committing "genocide." Rabbi Yaakov Menken, the executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, said in a statement to Fox News Digital, "To attempt to dress up Jew-hatred as a righteous cause is by no means new. No one is criticizing Rachel Accurso because she doesn't ‘want kids to be killed and starved.’" "She claims to care about 35.5 million children suffering from acute malnutrition across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia, but spends an inordinate amount of time speaking about 0.031 million children in Gaza," he added. "When 0.09% of starving children receive 90% of her attention, something is wrong." It is clear that her problem is not a deep concern for children, but that she is using her purported deep concern to mask something much darker," Menken concluded.

articles.title: Would-be Trump killer practiced 100-yard shot day before Pennsylvania assassination attempt, FBI documents show
articles.summary: Thomas Matthew Crooks struck Trump in the ear during a 2024 rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. He was subsequently shot dead by the Secret Service.
articles.body: Thomas Matthew Crooks became increasingly obsessed with guns and long-range shooting before he tried to assassinate Donald Trump on the campaign trail in July 2024, according to newly unclassified documents released by the FBI. Crooks, a 20-year-old engineering student, spent the day before he fired at Trump at the Clairton Sportsmen’s Club in Clairton, Pennsylvania, where he practiced shooting once a week on average, according to the federal files. He was a “terrible shot” at first, his father told investigators, according to documents cited by the New York Post, but he diligently practiced on his own and at shooting ranges. An employee at Keystone Shooting Center outside Pittsburgh described Crooks as “an odd duck” and “not someone they would want their daughter to spend time with,” federal investigators noted in the documents. A person at the Clairton gun club told investigators he remembered Crooks practicing a 100-yard shot the day before Trump’s speech in Butler, Pennsylvania. The collection of reports and interviews comprises 600 pages of interviews with Crooks’ relatives, neighbors, teachers and classmates. It also includes reports from responding law enforcement officers and details from the ensuing investigation. Together, the documents provide the first detailed look at Trump’s would-be assassin and his obsession with firearms, which Crooks’ father, Matthew Crooks, told investigators he developed during the Covid pandemic, according to the Post. Attempts to reach Matthew Crooks were unsuccessful Tuesday night. NBC News has not independently verified the documents the Post cited in its reporting on Crooks’ father, which the office of Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, said it showed the newspaper in person. NBC News requested the documents from Grassley, but his office did not provide them. In a brief interview Tuesday, Grassley said, “We don’t know anything about the motivation [of] why [Crooks] wanted to kill Trump.” One person was killed and two others were injured in the gunfire at the Butler Farm Show grounds. Crooks spent the months leading up to the Butler rally purchasing firearms and taking classes at Keystone Shooting Center, according to federal documents. He enrolled in basic and intermediate handgun courses and ordered gun parts online using the pseudonym Bob Dole, his father told investigators in an interview obtained by the Post. Matthew Crooks said his son perfected his aim over five years but showed no interest in outdoorsmanship, according to the Post. Instead, he mostly kept to himself and became increasingly withdrawn from his family, the Post reported. Crooks rarely showed emotions, his father told investigators, even when they argued, according to the paper. His son was described in federal documents by those who knew him, and whose names were redacted, as a history buff who could name all the U.S. presidents and enjoyed discussing the New Deal. Classmates told investigators Crooks was shocked that Trump was elected president in 2016 but otherwise discussed politics nonchalantly, according to the files. He was critical of both political parties despite being a registered Republican, and he donated $15 to the Democratic-run Progressive Turnout Project in 2021. “What makes Thomas ‘tic’ was his enjoyment in being ‘the smartest person in the room,’” investigators said. While he was enrolled at Bethel Park High School, Crooks did not appear to have close friends, and he was occasionally bullied, former classmates told investigators. The bullying “was never considered excessive, a chronic issue, or outside of normal High School behaviors.” However, Crooks “would ‘shut down’” around large groups of people or authority figures, the documents said. He also expressed interest in joining the armed services to work on nuclear submarines or with aircraft, his father told investigators. On July 13, 2024, Crooks waited six minutes into Trump’s campaign speech before he fired eight shots from an AR-15-style rifle. Trump was struck in the ear and pumped a fist into the air as blood trickled from his ear while Secret Service members swarmed around him, eventually leading him off the stage. Secret Service snipers pinpointed Crooks’ position on a rooftop outside the venue and killed him on the spot. Crooks had been planning to take engineering classes at Robert Morris University after having spent two years at the Community College of Allegheny County, where he received his associate degree, according to the newly released documents. Professors described him as a sharp student who was a delight in class, according to federal documents. A former roommate said Crooks kept an inconsistent sleep schedule and sometimes paced in the middle of the night. Crooks developed an interest in 3D printers and other electronic devices. He made small boats and “dragon eggs,” according to a former roommate cited in the federal investigation, and he created a home security camera using Raspberry Pi, which was originally used to teach computer science. Crooks worked at Bethel Park Nursing and Rehab as a dietary aide for about five years before the rally. Colleagues described him as an “‘odd, young kid’ who was sweet and ‘down to earth,’” federal investigators wrote. “He always did what was asked of him at work and never complained.” A co-worker said Crooks was last spotted at the nursing home on July 12, the day before Trump was shot, according to federal documents. Crooks had asked for the next day off and volunteered to work on July 14, instead. He was scheduled to take the morning shift.

articles.title: 40,000 bombs, $2.8 billion: Trump plans massive new arms package for Israel
articles.summary: International News: The Trump administration is planning a $2.8 billion arms package for Israel that would include 40,000 powerful 2,000lb bombs, weapons that were previo.
articles.body: The Trump administration is planning a $2.8 billion arms package for Israel that would include 40,000 powerful 2,000lb bombs, weapons that were previously withheld by the Biden administration over concerns about their potential to cause mass casualties in Gaza.The proposed deal includes 20,000 MK-84 bombs and 20,000 BLU-117s, according to US officials and a person familiar with the plan cited by The Guardian and Reuters. The package has not yet been finalised, but congressional committees have been informally notified about the proposed sale.Most of the package would reportedly be financed through US foreign military financing, under which US taxpayer funds are provided to Israel to purchase American-made weapons.The planned sale comes as Israel continues its military campaign in Gaza following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel, which killed around 1,200 people and saw 251 people taken hostage. Gaza's Health Ministry says more than 73,264 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's offensive, including those killed after the latest ceasefire took effect. Bombs once held back by BidenThe proposed deal marks another step by the Trump administration to expand Israel's access to US military equipment. In 2024, the Biden administration paused one shipment of MK-84 bombs over concerns about their use in densely populated areas of Gaza.Trump lifted that hold after returning to office in 2025. Last year, his administration also bypassed the normal congressional review process to approve a nearly $3 billion arms sale to Israel that included more than 35,500 of the 2,000lb bombs. In January, it approved another series of arms sales worth $6.67 billion.The 2,000lb bombs have several variants. Some are designed to penetrate underground targets, while others are intended for above-ground use and can cause extensive damage.Experts have previously linked US-made bombs to strikes in Gaza. Analysis of strike footage and blast fragments has indicated that such weapons were used against targets including suspected Hamas tunnel networks, while also causing deaths in densely populated areas.Trevor Ball, a former US Army explosive-ordnance-disposal technician who studies civilian harm caused by weapons, told The Washington Post that Israeli forces use MK-84 bombs to destroy entire buildings when targeting suspected militants.“If Hezbollah or whoever is in a building, an MK-84 will bring down the whole building,” Ball said.Deal comes amid continued Gaza strikesThe proposed sale comes despite a fragile ceasefire in Gaza, which has been violated repeatedly. Israel has continued carrying out strikes in the territory, including attacks overnight and into Tuesday that reportedly killed several people.Israel says its strikes are responses to shooting attacks by militants and other ceasefire violations. The conflict has also contributed to growing international pressure on Israel over its conduct of the war.Reuters reported that US public support for Israel has declined since the Gaza war began, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found that 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believed the US was too supportive of Israel, compared with 16% and 20%, respectively, when the question was first asked in 2017.Israel has maintained that its military actions are self-defence following the October 7 attack. A UN inquiry has accused Israel of genocide in Gaza, a charge Israel rejects.

articles.title: 3 dead after news helicopter reporting for NBC L.A. crashes while covering fatal bus collision
articles.summary: An NBC Los Angeles helicopter was covering a Los Angeles Metro bus and a passenger vehicle collision, which killed two people and injured others, fire officials said.
articles.body: A helicopter affiliated with NBC Los Angeles crashed while it was covering a fatal bus collision Tuesday evening, killing the photojournalist and pilot on board and one person on the ground, the station and officials said. The aircraft crashed in a parking lot at or near a self-storage facility in the community of Chatsworth, which is in Los Angeles’ San Fernando Valley, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department and news video on the ground from NBC Los Angeles. The helicopter was operated by Angel City Air and affiliated with the station, which broadcast that it had lost contact with those on board. “We knew it was a news chopper, we knew we’d lost contact with our people out there, and we’ve just received the confirmation that, in fact, NewsChopper 4 went down just before 7 o’clock tonight in Chatsworth,” anchor Colleen Williams said. “We’re going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, to process and to regroup,” Williams added, her voice becoming emotional. Angel City Air, which describes itself as “a full-service aerial production company,” did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday night. Three people were dead at the scene, and two others were taken to the hospital, Fire Battalion Chief Rico A. Gross said at a late-night news conference. Their conditions were unavailable. One of the deceased appeared to be a pedestrian on the ground when the crash happened, Fire Capt. Branden Silverman said earlier. The victims aboard the helicopter were identified by NBC Los Angeles as Angel City Air employees Eliana Moreno, an aerial photojournalist familiar to viewers of the station and its Spanish-language sister station, Telemundo 52, and pilot George Marciniw. Moreno was born in Orange County, south of L.A., and graduated from its Chapman University with a degree in broadcast journalism and political science in 2010, NBC Los Angeles reported. She joined Angel City Air’s helicopter team the same year and has reported for multiple Southern California news outlets. Marciniw also grew up in Southern California, where he graduated from Burbank High School, according to the station. NBC Los Angeles and Telemundo 52 issued a joint statement expressing condolences. “We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening,” the stations said. “We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.” The helicopter crash occurred after two people were killed and others were injured in a crash between a Los Angeles Metro bus and a passenger vehicle on Nordhoff Street, according to the fire department. It said that the bus crash happened at 5:03 p.m. and that firefighters worked to free the trapped people and assess the bus passengers. The helicopter was one of multiple aircraft covering the crash, NBC Los Angeles reported earlier. Fire and police personnel were nearby, Silverman said. They rushed to the crash, reported shortly before 7 p.m., and found the helicopter engulfed in flames, which had spread to nearby parked vehicles, he added. Witness Zareh Sevanesian was driving nearby with wife Allyona when he saw the chopper’s unusual descent. “As we were driving I looked over to my left,” he said. “I saw the helicopter — something didn’t look right. And I told my wife, ‘That helicopter is not flying right.’” Sevanesian said he saw the helicopter gradually losing altitude. Then, he said, he pulled over near the crash as fire roared. “It was one of the most violent fires I had ever seen,” Sevanesian recalled. He said he soon found a person down near the wreckage and three others “screaming uncontrollably.” “It was very terrifying and sad for everyone,” Allyona said. The fire department said the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration will be involved in the investigation. Speaking near the scene Tuesday night, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said it was “a heartbreaking night for our city.” She praised first responders for their quick reaction and expressed grief over those who were killed in the bus collision and the aircraft crash. “We lost five Angelenos today,” she said, “and my heart certainly goes out to the family and friends of all of those that we lost.” California Gov. Gavin Newsom also thanked first responders and offered condolences in a statement on X. “Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family,” he said.

articles.title: First-ever attack alert in Mecca sparks panic in Saudi; Muslim groups condemn Houthis
articles.summary: Middle East News: For the first time ever in the history of the Islamic holy city, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence issued an emergency alert warning of a possible hostile .
articles.body: For the first time ever in the history of the Islamic holy city, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence issued an emergency alert warning of a possible hostile aerial attack in Mecca.The alert advised residents to move indoors to safe locations and stay away from windows and doors until the danger had passed. Similar warnings were issued for Jeddah and Taif governorates.The alert was lifted within minutes, but it came as Saudi Arabia faces a widening security challenge from the Iran-backed Houthi group, which has intensified attacks on the kingdom while making territorial gains along Yemen’s strategically important Red Sea coast.The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) also condemned what it described as “heinous attacks” by the Houthis against Mecca and the Medina region, saying the attacks threatened civilians, violated the sanctity of holy sites and mosques, and provoked Muslims around the world.The OIC described attacks on holy sites, mosques and civilian infrastructure as terrorism and called such violations “unacceptable and intolerable”. It expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and backed measures taken by Riyadh to protect its security, sovereignty, civilians and the holy sites.Houthis however have outright denied targeting the holy city of Mecca, with a member of the group's political bureau calling Riyadh's claim a lie.Hizam al-Asad said in a post on X, "The fabrications and lies promoted by the criminal Al Saud regime regarding the targeting of the Honorable Mecca cannot deceive anyone, for it is they who desecrate it with debauchery and licentiousness and by importing prostitutes, and there is no threat from Yemen to the sanctities. Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites."But Mecca is only the most sensitive point in a much wider problem confronting Riyadh.From Mecca to Jazan: Pressure inside Saudi ArabiaThe latest alert followed a series of attacks and warnings across Saudi Arabia.On September 12, a projectile launched by Yemen’s Houthis landed in the Jazan region, injuring two people and damaging a mosque, several buildings and vehicles, according to Saudi Civil Defence.A day later, the Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen said Houthi forces had attacked civilian areas in Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif using ballistic missiles and drones.Coalition spokesperson Major General Turki Al-Maliki said 13 civilians suffered minor to moderate injuries, while seven residential homes and two vehicles were damaged. Saudi Arabia subsequently warned that it would respond to further attacks.Saudi authorities also issued alerts for Jeddah and Taif on Tuesday, ordering people to move indoors and stay away from windows and doors while the danger remained.Oil pipeline: A major pressure pointThe threat is not confined to missiles and drones targeting cities.On September 11, Saudi Arabia shut its 1,200-kilometre East-West oil pipeline after it was targeted in a drone attack launched from Iraq. No group claimed responsibility, while US President Donald Trump blamed Tehran, with Iranian proxies known to operate in Iraq, according to CNN.The pipeline has become particularly important because the war with Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. CNN reported that Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the East-West route to move around 5 million barrels of oil a day that would otherwise have been exported through the Persian Gulf.The attack therefore raised concerns in Riyadh about a wider campaign against critical Saudi infrastructure.CNN reported that Saudi Arabia had already been warned last month about the possibility of “multiple coordinated attacks” involving Iraqi militias working with the Iran-backed Houthis.The pipeline attack was not attributed to the Houthis, but it added to the broader pressure Saudi Arabia faces from Iran-aligned groups operating on multiple fronts.Red Sea: Houthis push towards a strategic chokepointAt the same time, the Houthis have been expanding their territorial reach in western Yemen.The group captured the strategic Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea and the port town of Mocha as it sought greater control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a key global shipping and energy route.Houthi media also reported that the group had captured fighters recruited by Saudi-backed forces who were stationed on the Red Sea islands of Hanish.The Hanish islands lie roughly 160 kilometres north of Bab al-Mandeb, close to routes linking the strait with the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.The advances give the Houthis greater strategic depth along a major maritime corridor while putting further pressure on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea interests.Why Riyadh is running out of roomThough Saudi Arabia has modern military and greater resources compared to a proxy group, the Houthis have shaped into a threat that needs to be taken seriously.Analysts cited by CNN said Riyadh does not want an all-out war but could increasingly be pushed towards one.Mohammed Al-Basha, a Yemen expert and Washington-based risk adviser, told CNN that signs pointed towards a large-scale Saudi retaliation and that “they don’t have an option”.Cinzia Bianco, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, told CNN that a major Saudi escalation could develop into an open-ended conflict similar to Yemen’s previous war.It could also pull Saudi Arabia deeper into the wider US-Iran conflict.That leaves Saudi Arabia looking for outside support while Washington appears reluctant to directly enter another fight.CNN reported that the US has resisted Saudi pressure to become directly involved militarily against the Houthis.Washington has, however, sent around 100 military advisers to Saudi Arabia to provide intelligence for its military campaign, according to multiple sources.US involvement also faces competing pressures, including the ongoing crisis around the Strait of Hormuz and domestic political considerations in Washington.Political exit is getting harderSaudi Arabia has so far shown what analysts describe as “strategic patience”, repeatedly warning and condemning the Houthis and Iran without launching a full-scale retaliation.After the East-West pipeline attack, the Saudi foreign ministry said the kingdom had chosen not to respond at that stage and would support efforts by the Iraqi government, while reserving the right to take measures necessary to protect its sovereignty.But Bianco told CNN that Saudi Arabia had “exhausted the political solutions”.The alternative, negotiating with the Houthis, could also carry a heavy political and strategic cost.Salman Al-Ansari, a Saudi geopolitical analyst, told CNN that the Saudi-backed Yemeni government’s military campaign against the Houthis was already underway and could intensify substantially in the coming days or even hours.He said there could be “major surprises on multiple fronts”.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Saudi Arabia says it shot down a Houthi drone near Mecca, Islam’s holiest city
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia said it shot down a Houthi drone on the outskirts of Islam’s holiest city Mecca on Tuesday –– prompting swift regional condemnation of the Iran-backed Yemeni rebel group.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia said it shot down a Houthi drone on the outskirts of Islam’s holiest city Mecca on Tuesday –– prompting swift regional condemnation of the Iran-backed Yemeni rebel group. It’s the first time that the Houthis have targeted Mecca in almost a decade, since a ballistic missile attack was intercepted in 2017, according to Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led Coalition Forces. The Houthis quickly denied threatening Mecca, with military spokesman Yahya Saree saying early Wednesday that its targets were Saudi oil facilities and military bases “far removed from the holy places.” The rebel group’s swift advance in Yemen and attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have put the Gulf Arab kingdom in an increasingly difficult position, facing the prospect of being drawn into a wider conflict, as the US-Iran war drags on. Mecca is the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad. All Muslims worldwide are required, if they are able, to make the pilgrimage to the holy city at least once in their life, with millions making the journey each year. “This hostile attempt will also remain a black mark in the record of violations by the extremist terrorist Houthi militia, as a deliberate act intended to provoke the feelings of millions of Muslims,” Al-Maliki said in a post on X, vowing to take the “necessary and deterrent measures” against the militants. The Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), a 57-member body representing 1.5 billion Muslims, also condemned the attempted attack, saying the attempted strikes “violate the sanctity of holy sites and mosques” and “instill fear in innocent civilians.” The prime minister of Pakistan – which recently recently signed a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia – called it a “dastardly and heinous” act. While Shehbaz Sharif did not mention the Houthis in his statement, he affirmed his country’s support for Saudi Arabia. The attack comes amid a flurry of fighting. The Houthis launched ballistic missiles and drones at several Saudi Arabian cities earlier this week, including Khamis Mushait, Abha, and Taif, injuring 13 civilians. And on Sunday, the Houthis claimed responsibility for an attack on a Saudi military base. In response, Saudi forces launched airstrikes across Houthi-held areas of Yemen last Saturday and this Tuesday, according to the Houthis. The Houthis have recently stepped up their fighting against Yemen’s Saudi-backed government and have expanded their area of control. Last week they captured a Red Sea port city in Yemen and an island near an important waterway that has, for months, acted as a backup to the Strait of Hormuz, allowing for the export of Saudi oil and refined products. That tightening grip over shipping in the Red Sea has fueled fears that the main escape valves for the region’s oil are slamming shut, as Iran and the US continue battling for control of the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices climbed back above $100 per barrel last week following further US strikes on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf and the fighting in Yemen – sparking protests around the world as people demand government action and economic relief.

articles.title: What’s the Pinglu Canal, China’s new gateway to Southeast Asia?
articles.summary: China’s first modern river-to-sea canal could significantly cut down time and costs of trade to Southeast Asia.
articles.body:
Beijing, China – China is opening its first modern river-to-sea canal for navigation on Wednesday, a project that aims to dramatically cut down shipping distances between the country’s southern hinterland and Southeast Asia, a region that serves as a critical trade partner.

The Pinglu Canal is located entirely in Guangxi, the region in China’s far south bordering Vietnam and overlooking the South China Sea.

This 134km (83-mile) waterway links the Xijiang River with the Beibu Gulf, the northwestern arm of the Gulf of Tonkin stretching between southern China and northern Vietnam. It gives vast areas of southwest China, including provinces such as Yunnan and Guizhou, a shorter route to the sea and to Asian markets.

The first such canal built by communist China, Pinglu is a part of the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor: A project involving southern Chinese provinces aimed at linking areas in western and southwestern China with Southeast Asian countries and global markets. The land-sea trade corridor is itself a part of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road Initiative, a web of highways, ports and railroads seeking to connect China with Europe and Africa.

The real gain: Savings in distance and cost

According to local authorities in Guangxi, the canal will shorten the shipping distance between inland areas of southwest China and Southeast Asian countries by about 560km (350 miles) and reduce logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent.

Estimates by Zhang Zhiwen, deputy secretary-general of the Guangxi government, indicate that transport costs alone will come down by more than 5 billion yuan annually, or about $700m.

The region’s vice chairwoman, Lu Xinning, describes these returns as “tangible gains” that reduce operating costs and boost domestic and foreign trade.

The canal will allow the passage of ships with a capacity of 5,000 tonnes. Its estimated cost is about 72.7 billion yuan, equivalent to about $10.8bn.

This means cities and industrial areas far from the coast in southwest China will become closer to maritime trade routes. The new trade corridor does not serve Guangxi alone; it is connected to a broader network extending to Chongqing in southwest China, Chengdu in Sichuan province, Guizhou and Yunnan, before goods reach the ports of the Beibu Gulf and, from there, overseas markets.

These changes come at a time when trade between China and Southeast Asia is growing rapidly. According to China’s General Administration of Customs, bilateral trade in the first half of 2026 reached about 4.34 trillion yuan, or about $640bn, an increase of 18.2 percent year on year.

At the southern end of the canal, container-handling capacity at Beibu Gulf Port rose from 2.28 million TEUs in 2017 to 10.06 million TEUs in 2025, with a shipping network covering major Southeast Asian ports.

Guangxi is also working to build what it calls the “Pinglu Canal Economic Belt”, with the aim of attracting industries and spreading them out along the new corridor, while linking them to ports, transport networks and supply chains.

The targeted sectors include non-ferrous metals and critical minerals, modern green chemicals, as well as artificial intelligence and information technology. Industrial zones are also being developed near ports, reducing the distance between production sites and shipping centres.

The process of organising and directing shipping sources has already begun to generate new commercial activity. A train loaded with sodium bisulfate recently arrived from Chongqing, the major industrial and transport hub in southwest China, at the port of Nanning, the capital of Guangxi province. After the canal opens, direct commercial sailings are scheduled to begin to the port of Can Tho in southern Vietnam.

On the operational front, Guangxi has adopted a tiered transit-fee system that gives operators a grace period before imposing nominal charges.

Until December 31, 2026, commercial vessels will pass through the three water gates along the canal completely free of charge. Starting January 1, 2027, a fee of one yuan, about $0.14, will be charged for each tonne of a vessel’s capacity every time it passes through these gates. This trial rate will remain in effect until September 2031.

River vessels can sail directly to the berths of Qinzhou seaport without needing to transfer their cargo to other ships, enabling a seamless transition from river to sea.

Resettlement: Another side of the canal project

Building a canal of this scale would not have been possible without addressing a sensitive human dimension: Relocating thousands of families from their land. According to official sources, the resettlement process involved 2,764 households comprising 11,228 people across four counties and county-level cities in Guangxi. In Hengzhou alone, evacuation agreements were signed for 368 homes, which were completely demolished over a total area of 84,200 square metres (906,321 square feet), with 1,221 people temporarily resettled.

The process was not managed solely through financial compensation. Instead, 21 different housing models were designed in accordance with residents’ customs: The orientation of reception rooms, crop-drying areas, poultry enclosures and storage rooms for agricultural chemicals. In Shaping, the largest town in the resettlement project, residents were given four-storey homes covering 420sq metres (4,520sq ft), some with commercial storefronts facing the street.

Still, there is a sense of loss among many, even if mitigated by hope for the future.

In Xinfu, where the village of Fenghuangping once stood, one resident who was forced to leave said: “There is no longer a village called Fenghuangping, but with the Pinglu Canal, tomorrow will be better.”

Some families moved seven-century-old trees to the new site of their homes, including a 217-year-old camphor tree.

The resettlement process was carried out within 39 days, but it was linked to promises of jobs at the construction site and vocational training for residents of the relocated areas.

How geography is reshaping trade security

Straits and maritime corridors have long been the arteries of power in the global economy, but they are also among its most sensitive points of weakness.

The Hormuz crisis embodies this paradox: The passageway through which about one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies flow can, when threatened, become a factor that paralyses trade and redraws its routes.

Faced with that backdrop, countries around the world are trying to develop alternative routes and supply chains – pipelines, storage facilities and transport corridors that reduce the dependence of nations on just one or two routes.

The Pinglu Canal is China’s latest endeavour to do just that: Build an alternative, shorter and faster route to a critical market.

articles.title: South Yorkshire fire chief calls for long-term plan to tackle wildfires
articles.summary: Chief Fire Officer Chris Kirby urges action to reflect the 'changing nature of emergencies'.
articles.body:
South Yorkshire's chief fire officer has called on the government to create a long-term strategy to tackle wildfires in the UK.

Between June and August, South Yorkshire experienced 53 wildfires, as five official heatwaves made it the hottest summer on record.

Chris Kirby, of South Yorkshire Fire & Rescue Service (SYFRS), called for a strategy that "reflects the changing nature of emergencies facing the UK".

The government-funded UK Wildfire Conference will be held in Leeds in November, to discuss how prepared the nation is to prevent and respond to wildfires.

This summer, the number of emergency 999 calls was up 84% and the number of incidents increased by 39% compared to averages of the previous three summers, according to SYFRS.

Kirby said the strategy must include "sustained investment in firefighters, specialist wildfire capabilities, training, equipment and national resilience improvements".

Wildfires were no longer confined to remote rural areas, Kirby said, and "as fires move from open land into urban and suburban communities, they are threatening homes, businesses and critical infrastructure".

"When we are responding to wildfires, they can go on for days, if not weeks, and all of a sudden it puts a real strain on the fire and rescue service," Kirby said.

"We need to have a long, careful look at the whole arrangement of how we are prepared for these kind of incidents across the fire and rescue services and it's a conversation that I'm really pleased that government are willing to have."

Unlike other nations, the UK does not have a fire and rescue service asset that allows services to deploy water from an aircraft in the event of a large wildfire.

Kirby said that local contractual arrangements had allowed some services to "receive some well-needed aerial firefighting capability".

"But really we need to tighten up on that arrangement and I'm sure that that's something that will be discussed at length at the upcoming wildfire summit that the government have promised to host."

articles.title: UK inflation pushed up by petrol and diesel price rises
articles.summary: Summer holidays and disruption to global oil supplies by the Middle East conflict stoked price growth.
articles.body:
Rises in petrol, diesel and airfares pushed UK inflation up to its highest level in six months in the year to August.

Inflation accelerated to 3.1% from 2.9% , according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The cost of filling up a vehicle soared in August as the conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt global oil supplies. Petrol prices jumped to their highest for nearly four years, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.

Meanwhile, the cost of flying jumped during the key month for summer getaways.

Overall, motor fuel prices rose by 23% compared to August last year.

Oil hit more than $91 a barrel as the US-Israel war with Iran went on. That compares to around $73 just before hostilities began earlier this year.

As a result, average petrol prices have continued to climb and between July and August, they rose by 9.1p to 161.3p per litre.

"This is the highest price recorded since November 2022," said the ONS. At that point, Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine had pushed up global energy costs.

Capital Economics said, at this point, the effect of higher oil prices has not spilled over into other areas such as food and drink, where the pace of inflation remained at 1.3% in the year to August.

But its chief UK economist, Paul Dales, said: "Everyone knows that bigger rises in inflation are on their way."

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said: "Rising crude oil and petrol prices increased both the annual cost of raw materials and the price of goods leaving factories respectively."

Dales estimates that a combination of higher oil and gas prices and "the eventual 'first-round' effect of businesses passing on some of their higher energy costs" will lead to inflation peaking at 4.2% in January.

As well as hitting drivers in the pocket, higher oil prices also affect forecourts.

Goran Raven, owner of Essex petrol station RJ Raven, told the BBC: "Things are down. We've got lots of pressure on us at the moment. I'd say we're about 20% down on this time last year."

Raven said changes in the oil price have a "real-time impact on us".

In recent days, Brent crude - the global benchmark for oil prices - has surpassed $100 a barrel.

"We only have small tanks here, so we need a tanker almost every day at the moment and we have to pay a daily spot price," said Raven. "When the price goes up, we have to go up with it. There's no way around it.

"The margins here are wafer-thin on fuel. People like to think we're earning a lot on it. Unfortunately, we really aren't. It's single digits of pence we earn per litre."

The rise in inflation means it has moved further away from the Bank of England's 2% target.

The bank uses interest rates to control inflation.

The rate currently stands at 3.75% and the Bank of England is meeting on Thursday to decide whether to change it.

Chancellor John Healey, who is preparing to announce his first Budget next month, said: "The war in the Middle East is impacting on inflation worldwide, not just here at home. In our bills, our weekly shop and at the petrol pumps."

He said: "Despite this serious global uncertainty, our UK economy is proving resilient."

The most recent figures showed that the UK economy expanded by 0.4% in July , boosted by investment in artificial intelligence.

But, for the second quarter between April and June, Britain's economic growth slowed to 0.4% from 0.6% in January to March.

articles.title: Rescued moon bears arrive at Jimmy's Farm & Wildlife Park
articles.summary: The bears, rescued from a bile farm, are beginning their new lives in a wildlife park
articles.body:
Five moon bears that spent decades living in cages in South Korea have arrived at their new home in Suffolk.

Jimmy's Farm & Wildlife Park near Ipswich and its charity, Space for the Wild, transported the animals 5,500 miles (8,850km) to their new forever home at the park.

The bears, which arrived on Thursday, had been kept at one of South Korea's last bear bile farms – sites which have now been banned in the country.

Jimmy Doherty, founder of the wildlife park, said the bears would now live a "profoundly better life".

"I will never forget meeting the bears for the first time," he said.

"It was truly hell on earth. You cannot unsee these things.

"It made us all the more determined and focused on our mission - to get these bears safe, protected and living a profoundly better life.

"The work, dedication and public support of so many have made this a reality. I couldn't be more grateful to all involved."

The rescued bears - Bara, Rumi, Saebit, Yonggi and Huimang - are enjoying a new reserve at the park created specifically for them.

It includes space for them to climb, swim and rest among trees and grass.

The park launched a campaign to fund the rescue and has raised more than £90,000 out of a target of £200,000.

South Korea banned the breeding and possession of the bears last year, along with the extraction of bile from their gallbladders.

The bile was used in medicines while the bears themselves were often kept in poor conditions.

articles.title: US military releases footage of massive operation to rescue injured airman stranded inside Iran
articles.summary: Newly released video from the US military shows elite Air Force pararescue operators rescuing an injured F-15E Strike Eagle crewman stranded deep inside Iran earlier this year.
articles.body: The U.S. military released dramatic new video on Tuesday showing parts of one of the largest combat search-and-rescue operations in its history, including the moment elite Air Force pararescue operators reached a badly injured American airman stranded deep inside Iran. The footage documents portions of the massive April operation to rescue the two-man crew of an F-15E Strike Eagle, call sign Dude 44, after the fighter was shot down by an Iranian shoulder-fired missile. The pilot, known as Dude44 Alpha, and the backseat weapons systems officer, Dude44 Bravo, ejected from the aircraft and landed miles apart, leaving both stranded inside Iran. While Dude44 Alpha was rescued after a little more than six hours, Dude44 Bravo suffered a broken back, arm and shoulder after a damaged parachute led to a hard landing. He remained stranded for nearly two days before U.S. forces reached him. HOLLYWOOD LEGEND MAKING MOVIE ABOUT EPIC IRAN RESCUE MISSION TO SAVE F-15 FIGHTER JET CREW The newly released video shows U.S. military helicopters searching for Bravo as American forces worked to locate and recover him. Despite his injuries, Bravo moved away from his landing site and began climbing toward a roughly 7,000-foot ridgeline as daylight revealed the desert valley and steep cliffs surrounding him. The footage also shows American bombers and drones striking Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces that were in close proximity to Bravo. TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS "There was clear intent out of the Iranian ground force to come find those two guys," Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine told CBS News this week. The video then shows the dramatic moment on April 5 when two elite Air Force pararescue operators, known as PJs, reached the injured Bravo on the mountain ridgeline. Two large search-and-rescue aircraft had landed on a makeshift desert runway before smaller "Little Bird" helicopters flew toward Bravo's position on the ridgeline. Bravo called the moment he saw his rescuers "one of the greatest moments of my life." HOW IRAN ATTACKS ARE FORCING THE PENTAGON TO RETHINK ITS DECADES-OLD MIDDLE EAST BASE STRATEGY "Let's go," he recalled telling them. The second rescue operation put 92 U.S. service members on the ground in Iran, marking the first time American forces had boots on the ground in the country since 1980. Hundreds of U.S. service members also supported the operation from the air, while between 3,000 and 5,000 service members supported the rescue mission overall, according to U.S. Central Command Commander Adm. Brad Cooper. But the operation was not over once Bravo was reached. The landing gear of the two rescue aircraft became trapped in the desert sand, stranding Bravo and more than 90 U.S. service members inside Iran. A clandestine Air Force unit was ultimately brought in to extract the group, CBS News reported. Bravo was finally brought to safety roughly 50 hours after Dude 44 was shot down. The rescue was completed as the sun rose on Easter Sunday. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Liz Friden and Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price contributed to this report.
